When does Shopify Grow beat Basic?

Merchants search this because Grow’s monthly bill is higher, but the processing rates on the plan picker are usually lower. The only number that turns that into a decision is volume: extra monthly plan cost divided by what each order saves in fees on your payment path.

This page uses the same illustrative US online defaults as the Shopify fee calculator. Replace them with the rates on your current statements. It does not publish Shopify’s live schedule and it does not recommend a plan — higher tiers also change features this arithmetic cannot see.

Your volume and payment path

Calculating…

Plan Monthly Fees / order Fee + plan / month vs Basic

“vs Basic” here is the monthly fee-and-plan gap, not net profit. Cost of goods is the same on every plan, so it cancels. Open the full calculator to include shipping you pay, packaging, and a target margin.

The arithmetic

On the illustrative defaults, Grow is $66 more per month than Basic ($105 − $39). Shopify Payments drops from 2.9% to 2.7% on the same $54 order — eleven cents. $66 ÷ $0.108 is about 612 orders/month before Grow’s rates cover the extra subscription.

On a third-party path the Shopify transaction fee often drops as well (2% → 1% on those same defaults). That is 54 cents more saved on the same $54 order, so Grow can cover the extra $66 at a much lower volume. If most checkouts already use Shopify Payments, use that path; if they use PayPal, use that one. Mixing them needs a weighted average you can approximate by changing the order total and volume.

Advanced and Plus follow the same rule: extra monthly cost divided by per-order fee savings. The full calculator ranks all four plans on your real costs, not just fees.

Common questions

When does upgrading from Shopify Basic to Grow pay for itself?

Grow costs more each month and usually charges a lower Shopify Payments rate and a lower third-party transaction fee. It starts paying from those rates alone when monthly orders times the per-order fee savings exceed the extra monthly plan cost. Enter the rates from your statements — this page does not publish Shopify's live schedule.

Does PayPal change the Basic vs Grow break-even?

Yes. On a third-party processor path, Shopify's extra transaction fee often drops when you move up a plan, so the per-order savings can be larger than on Shopify Payments and Grow can cover its extra monthly cost at a lower volume.

What this checks

Merchants search “Shopify post purchase upsell” because a $18 add-on looks like free leftover and a one-click after they paid looks free. A second 2.9% + $0.30 on $16.20 is $0.77. A $0.50 extra pack is not the hero box. A 2% extra abandon on a $31.74 ticket is $0.63 — enough to flip a thin checkout lead.

On the defaults — $48 item, $6 shipping charged, $18 add-on at 10% off ($16.20), $6 add-on cost, Basic 2.9% + $0.30, $14 cost, $5 + $1 ship, $39 / 100 plan, 18% checkout take, 12% one-click take, 2% extra abandon, 80 checkouts — skipping keeps $31.74. If they add at checkout the combined leftover is $40.97. After the 18% take and 2% drop, checkout expects $32.74 ($0.99 more). One-click expects $32.82 ($1.07 more, $8.93 on the second swipe) — $0.08 more than checkout, $85.73 / month versus skipping. Checkout take has to land about 7.0% before it matches skipping. One-click take has to land about 11.1% before it matches the checkout offer. Extra abandon can rise to about 1.8% before checkout matches one-click. Drop the extra abandon to 0% and checkout expects $33.41 against $32.82 on one-click.

It does not tell you to install an upsell app, and it is not tax or financial advice. A cart they already left is a different question — leave vs recovery emails vs a coupon. A subscribe-and-save on the same SKU is on one-time vs monthly vs a prepaid pack. A checkout they already completed is on Shop Pay Installments vs the card. The main Shopify fee calculator still compares Shopify Payments with PayPal.

Common questions

Should I add a Shopify post-purchase upsell?

A one-click add-on after they already paid keeps the hero leftover and adds a second swipe. On the calculator defaults ($48 item, $18 add-on at 10% off, 2.9%+$0.30, 18% checkout take, 12% one-click take, 2% extra abandon) skipping keeps $31.74, the checkout offer expects $32.74, and one-click expects $32.82. That is arithmetic on your inputs, not advice to install an upsell app.

Does a Shopify checkout upsell beat a post-purchase offer?

The first swipe saves a second $0.30 and one plan allocation. A 2% extra abandon can wipe that lead. On the defaults, checkout keeps $0.99 more than skipping if they still pay, but after the 2% drop one-click keeps $0.08 more ($32.82 vs $32.74). Drop the extra abandon to 0% and checkout expects $33.41.

When does a Shopify upsell lose money?

When the add-on leftover after the discount, second card fee, and extra pack is negative, or when the checkout offer's extra abandon zeros tickets that would have completed. Checkout take has to land about 7.0% on the defaults before it matches skipping. Recovering a cart they already left is a different comparison.

Should I collect duties on Shopify?

vs-a-flat-card-fee-guess.html.text:
← Shopify Fee & Profit Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat card-fee guess

"Just take off 2.9% and 30 cents" is the card-fee rule every merchant already knows. It can be the exact processing fee on one payment path — and it is never the profit, and it is never right at all on the other path.

What the flat card-fee guess is

Almost every merchant carries the same rule of thumb for what a card purchase costs to process: take about 2.9% off the top, then another 30 cents. It is fast, it needs no tool, and it is close enough for a gut check on a single sale.

The trouble is what it was never built to do. It prices one thing — the processing fee — and assumes that fee is the same whatever processor actually touches the order. It has no line for cost of goods, the shipping label you pay for, packaging, or the slice of your monthly Shopify plan that order should carry. And it has no way to know that Shopify itself can add a second fee on top of the processor's, whenever the order does not run through Shopify Payments.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the item price, shipping charged, cost of goods, shipping you pay, packaging, the monthly Shopify plan allocated across your expected monthly orders, and the processing rates from your own statements — the Shopify Payments rate, the Shopify third-party transaction rate, and your processor's rate and fixed fee. It runs the order through Shopify Payments and a third-party processor side by side and reports what each path actually leaves, not just what each path charges in fees.

OrderFlat guess ("2.9% + 30 cents") profitReal profit, Shopify PaymentsReal profit, third-party

$150 item + $12 shipping, higher cost of goods and packaging$157.00$85.61$81.23

Worked using this calculator's own arithmetic (calculateOrder) at 2.9% + $0.30 Shopify Payments, a 2% Shopify third-party transaction fee, and a 3.49% + $0.49 processor — the calculator's own shipped defaults, not numbers invented for this page. Open the calculator to check either row yourself.

Notice that the flat guess gets closer to nothing as the order gets more realistic. Both rows use the same $1.87 or $5.00 processing-fee estimate the rule of thumb would give — and both real numbers still fall well short, because cost of goods, shipping, packaging, and the plan cost never entered the guess at all.

What a flat card-fee guess doesWhat this calculator does instead
Assumes one flat percentage plus fixed fee applies to every order, whatever the actual payment path. Runs the order through Shopify Payments and a third-party processor side by side, using the rates and any extra Shopify third-party transaction fee you enter.
Has no line for the extra Shopify transaction fee that a third-party processor can trigger on top of its own rate. Adds that fee to the third-party path automatically, and reports the exact extra cost versus Shopify Payments on the same order.
Stops at the fee, so "revenue minus fee" quietly gets treated as profit. Nets out cost of goods, the shipping you actually pay, packaging, and a share of the monthly Shopify plan before calling anything profit.
Cannot say what to charge to hit a margin or a dollar-profit target. Reports the break-even price and the price that clears a target margin or a target net profit, on either path.
Gives one number for "the fee," with no separate reading for Shopify Payments and a third-party processor. Shows both paths' fee and profit at once, so switching processors is a number to check rather than a guess.

A flat card-fee guess is not wrong because it is simple — on Shopify Payments, at Shopify's own Basic-plan rate, it can even land on the exact fee. It is wrong the moment "the fee" gets treated as "the profit," and it is wrong again the moment the order runs through a processor other than Shopify Payments, because that guess was never built to see Shopify's own extra fee. This calculator does not replace judgment about your prices; it replaces the arithmetic a flat guess skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat "2.9% + 30 cents" guess get Shopify profit wrong?

Because it only estimates the processing fee, and even then only for one payment path. On this calculator's own default order (a $48 item plus $6 shipping), that guess happens to land on the exact fee Shopify Payments charges — $1.87 — because 2.9% and 30 cents are also Shopify Payments' Basic-plan rate. But the fee is not the profit: cost of goods, the shipping you actually pay, packaging, and a share of the monthly plan still come out of the order, and a flat guess has no line for any of them.

What does the guess miss when the store uses a third-party processor?

The extra Shopify third-party transaction fee. When an order runs through a third-party processor instead of Shopify Payments, Shopify can add its own transaction fee on top of the processor's rate. On this calculator's default order that pushes the real fee to $3.45 — $1.59 more than the flat guess — and on a $150 item plus $12 shipping the gap widens to $4.39 per order, $438.58 across 100 orders a month.

How much does the guess overstate profit, in dollars?

On this calculator's own default order, a flat 2.9% + 30 cents guess says the order nets $52.13. The real payout is $31.74 on Shopify Payments and $30.16 on a third-party processor — the guess overstates profit by $20.39 and $21.98. On a heavier order (a $150 item plus $12 shipping, with higher cost of goods, shipping, and packaging), the guess says $157.00 while the real payout is $85.61 and $81.23 — a $71.39 to $75.78 overstatement.

Is the flat guess ever close?

Only for the fee itself, and only on Shopify Payments — because Shopify Payments' own Basic-plan rate is 2.9% + 30 cents, the same numbers the rule of thumb uses. It has never been close on profit, because it has no line for cost of goods, shipping you pay, packaging, or the plan cost per order, and it has never been close on the fee for a third-party processor, because it does not know Shopify's extra transaction fee exists.

Does this calculator know Shopify's current published rates?

No. It does not publish or assume a live Shopify rate card. You enter the Shopify Payments rate, the third-party transaction rate, and your processor's rate and fixed fee from your own statements, and it runs the arithmetic on both paths side by side — the same arithmetic a flat guess skips, not a claim about what Shopify currently charges.

Nothing here says or implies that using a flat card-fee guess is a mistake to feel bad about — it is a common, honest shortcut that works for a quick gut check and stops working the moment it gets treated as the order's actual profit. This calculator vs. doing it in a spreadsheet

Names no spreadsheet application or company. Your management system already gives you the rates; the arithmetic is not hard. Here is exactly where a hand-built Shopify fee sheet quietly picks the wrong number, worked against the same $66 order this calculator would price.

First — a spreadsheet is the right tool for tracking

A row per order, or per month, tied to your own Shopify and processor exports is how you watch a trend across a quarter. This calculator keeps no history at all: close the tab and the order is gone. If what you need is last month's numbers, or twelve months of them side by side, your spreadsheet already does that better than this page ever will.

What follows is not an argument that the fee math is hard. It is four places a formula built by hand quietly gives you a number you cannot act on, each shown against the same worked order.

The worked order

One Shopify Basic order: a $60.00 item, $6.00 shipping charged to the customer ($66.00 revenue), $22.00 cost of goods, $7.20 to ship it, $1.10 packaging, and a $39/month Basic plan. Shopify Payments runs 2.9% + $0.30; the comparison processor runs a published 3.49% + $0.30 — plus, on Basic, Shopify's own 2% third-party transaction fee on top, which is the part a hand formula built from the processor's rate card alone leaves out.

QuestionSpreadsheet built from rate cardsThis calculator
Profit on Shopify Payments $66.00 − ($60.00×2.9%+$0.30) − $30.56 = $33.23 — correct, and the same figure this page reports $33.23, 50.3% margin
Profit on the third-party processor $32.65 — the processor's own 3.49% + $0.30 only $31.33 — the processor's rate plus Shopify's own 2% third-party transaction fee ($1.32) that the rate card does not carry
How much more the third-party path really costs $0.58 of profit — underweighted, because the missing $1.32 fee is a cost on both paths' difference $1.90 of profit — about 3.3× the spreadsheet's gap
Per-order profit at 150 orders/month $33.23, plan cost tracked as separate monthly overhead $33.23 — plan cost of $0.26 already folded in
The same order at 10 orders/month Still $33.23, if the plan line stays separate from per-order profit $29.59 — a $3.64 swing, because $39 spread across 10 orders is $3.90 each, not $0.26
Price needed for a 30% margin $30.56 ÷ (1−30%) = $43.66 — cost divided by one minus the margin, fee left out of the denominator $39.99 — the fee percentage shares the same denominator as the margin, so it is not added on top twice
Minimum (break-even) item price $31.78 — the full covering-cost total, shipping charged left in $25.78 — the $6.00 the customer already pays for shipping is netted back out first
Where the numbers go Your file, your machine Also your machine — the arithmetic runs in your browser and nothing you type is uploaded

The four places a hand formula goes quiet

1. The rate card is not the whole third-party fee

A processor's own published rate — 3.49% + $0.30 in this worked order — is not what a third-party checkout actually costs on Shopify. On plans below Plus, Shopify adds its own third-party transaction fee (2% on Basic, falling to 1% on Grow, 0.5% on Advanced, and 0% only on Plus) on the same order total. Leave it out and the $66.00 order's true third-party fee of $4.11 reads as $2.79 — which shrinks the real $1.90 profit gap between Shopify Payments and the outside processor down to $0.58, about a third of the true number. The direction of the decision does not change on this order, but the size of it does, and a merchant weighing whether switching processors is worth the hassle is weighing the wrong number either way.

2. A monthly plan fee has to be divided by that month's orders

$39 a month is not a line you can leave off a per-order number and still call it profit — it is cash that month's orders have to cover between them, and how many orders there are changes how much each one owes. At 150 orders a month the same $66.00 order nets $33.23 after $0.26 of allocated plan cost; at 10 orders a month, the identical order nets $29.59, because the same $39 now allocates to $3.90. A spreadsheet that tracks "plan cost" as separate overhead, rather than dividing it into each order's own fee line, hides a swing that is largest for exactly the low-volume stores a plan-upgrade decision matters most for.

3. A target-margin price is not cost ÷ (1 − margin)

That formula is correct when nothing else in the sale scales with price. A payment-processing fee does: it is a percentage of whatever price you land on, so it belongs in the same denominator as the margin you are solving for, not added afterward. On this order, cost ÷ (1−30%) says $43.66; the price that actually clears a 30% margin once the 2.9% fee is priced in is $39.99. Priced from the naive formula, this order is $3.67 more expensive than it needs to be to hit the same target — a real cost in a competitive listing, for a margin the correct price already delivers.

4. A break-even price still has to net shipping back out

The $6.00 a customer pays for shipping is revenue, and it already goes toward covering the order's costs — so the item price alone does not have to carry the whole covering-cost total. A break-even formula that solves for the full amount and stops there puts the floor at $31.78; netting the $6.00 shipping charge back out (the step this calculator's own algebra always takes) puts it at $25.78. Skip that step and every break-even and minimum-price figure a spreadsheet reports is high by however much the customer is already paying for shipping.

When your spreadsheet is still the better tool

For tracking, always. This page prices one order at a time and remembers nothing between visits. A sheet with a row per order, or per month, tied to your own Shopify and processor exports is how you watch realized margin move across a quarter, catch a rate that changed, or see which SKU is quietly thin. The two are not competing tools: use this calculator to get one order's arithmetic right and see the four places above before you build the formula, then keep tracking the results in the sheet you already have.

Every figure on this page comes from this calculator's own worked example, not a claim about Shopify's current published rates or any specific processor's schedule. Enter the rates from your own statements — the numbers above illustrate where a formula goes wrong, not what you will be charged.

Common questions

Can I just build a Shopify fee spreadsheet myself?

Yes, and for tracking a month at a time you should — a spreadsheet's real strength is a row per order or per month tied to your own export, which this calculator does not keep. What a hand-built sheet quietly gets wrong is the arithmetic inside one row: the extra Shopify third-party transaction fee on top of a processor's own rate, the monthly plan cost that has to be divided across orders rather than left off as overhead, and the algebra for a target-margin or break-even price, which is not a single division.

Why does my spreadsheet understate how much more PayPal or Stripe costs than Shopify Payments?

Because Shopify charges its own third-party transaction fee — 2% on the Basic plan — on top of whatever PayPal, Stripe or another processor charges, and a formula built from the processor's published rate alone never includes it. On this page's worked $66 order that fee is $1.32 by itself. A spreadsheet missing it shows Shopify Payments beating a third-party processor by $0.58 of profit; the true gap, once Shopify's own cut is added, is $1.90 — about 3.3 times larger.

Why does my per-order profit look different at low volume than at high volume?

The monthly plan fee has to be divided by that month's order count, not treated as a separate overhead line, because it is cash that specific month's orders have to cover between them. On this page's worked order, a $39/month Basic plan allocates to $0.26 at 150 orders a month but $3.90 at 10 orders a month — a $3.64 profit swing on the identical sale, from volume alone. A spreadsheet that tracks the plan fee separately from per-order profit hides that swing.

Why is the price my spreadsheet says I need for a target margin too high?

Because "cost divided by (1 minus the target margin)" leaves out that the processing fee is also a percentage of the final price, not a cost paid before the fee is taken. Solving for the correct price means the fee percentage and the target margin both come out of the same denominator. On this page's worked order that omission overprices the item by $3.67 — a spreadsheet says $43.66, the correct target-margin price is $39.99.

Why does my break-even price come out too high?

Because the shipping a customer pays at checkout is revenue that already goes toward covering costs, and a break-even formula that solves for the full order total rather than netting that shipping back out overstates the minimum item price by the full amount charged for shipping. On this page's worked order that is $6.00 — a spreadsheet that skips the step says $31.78 is the floor; it is actually $25.78.

Which Shopify promo still pays: 10% off, $10 off, or free shipping

Merchants treat “10% off,” “$10 off,” and “free shipping” as similar generosity. They are not. Shopify Payments and PayPal take a percentage of item plus shipping charged. A percent-off coupon shrinks that base. Free shipping sets shipping charged to $0 and leaves the label you actually pay on the order.

On a typical Basic-plan example — a $48 item, $6 shipping charged, a $5 label, $14 goods, $1 pack, and 2.9% + $0.30 Shopify Payments — list price keeps about $31.74. The same order under three common sales:

OfferCustomer paysFeesYou keep
List price$54.00$1.87$31.74
10% off the item$49.20$1.73$27.08
Free shipping$48.00$1.69$25.92
$10 off the item$44.00$1.58$22.03

If a sale has to run, 10% off keeps about $1.17 more than free shipping on that order. Free shipping is the one that can flip a thin listing to a loss: a $24 item with a $9 label and $10 shipping charged still profits under 10% off and loses money when shipping is advertised as free.

Rates change by country, plan, card type, and contract. This page does not publish Shopify’s live schedule. Open the Shopify fee calculator, enter the percentages from your statements, and compare the four offers on one order.

The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend a sale or claim a promo will increase volume enough to make up the difference.

Common questions

Is free shipping cheaper than 10% off on Shopify?

Not on orders where the label is a large share of the advertised discount. A 10% coupon cuts the item price, so Shopify Payments or PayPal percentage fees also drop. Free shipping sets shipping charged to $0 and leaves the label you pay on the order. Run both against your costs before you pick a sale.

Why does a $10 coupon take more profit than 10% off?

On a $48 item, 10% off is $4.80 and a $10 coupon is $10. Both also change the order total that percentage processing fees apply to. The calculator shows the net after fees, goods, and the label — not the face value of the discount.

why-paypal-costs-more.html.text:
← Shopify fee calculator

Why PayPal can cost more than Shopify Payments on the same order

Merchants search for “Shopify PayPal fees” because a checkout that uses PayPal, Stripe, or another processor is not just that processor’s rate. Shopify may also charge a third-party transaction fee on the order total. Shopify Payments replaces that extra Shopify fee with the Shopify Payments processing rate.

On a typical Basic-plan example — a $50 item, 2% Shopify third-party fee, and a 3.49% + $0.49 processor — the third-party path pays both the processor and Shopify. The Shopify Payments path pays only the Payments rate (for example 2.9% + $0.30). The difference is cash the merchant keeps or gives away on every order.

Rates change by country, plan, card type, and contract. This page does not publish Shopify’s live schedule. Open the Shopify fee calculator, enter the percentages from your current statements, and compare both paths on one order — including shipping, cost of goods, and a share of the monthly plan.

Refunds change the comparison again: PayPal often keeps its processing fee when the order is reversed. What a refund rate still leaves mixes completed-order profit with a full-refund outcome on both paths.

The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend a processor or claim a store is more profitable after switching.
